problems.title: Paid orders
problems.prompt: Return paid order IDs and amounts, ordered by ID.
problems.solution: SELECT id,amount FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY id
problems.explanation: Filter before presenting the result. Cancelled orders are excluded.

problems.title: Order owners
problems.prompt: Return each order ID and its customer name, ordered by order ID.
problems.solution: SELECT o.id,c.name FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id ORDER BY o.id
problems.explanation: Join on the foreign key rather than names; customer names need not be unique.

problems.title: Customers without orders
problems.prompt: Return customer names with no orders of any status, ordered by name.
problems.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id) ORDER BY c.name
problems.explanation: NOT EXISTS checks absence directly. Cancelled orders still count as orders for this prompt.

problems.title: Paid spending per customer
problems.prompt: Include every customer with total paid spending; use 0 when none. Order by customer ID.
problems.solution: SELECT c.name,COALESCE(SUM(o.amount),0)::int total FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid' GROUP BY c.id,c.name ORDER BY c.id
problems.explanation: Keep the status condition in ON so customers without paid orders survive the LEFT JOIN.

problems.title: Repeat paying customers
problems.prompt: Return customer IDs having at least two paid orders, ordered by customer ID.
problems.solution: SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING COUNT(*)>=2 ORDER BY customer_id
problems.explanation: WHERE selects paid rows first; HAVING then filters the grouped counts.

problems.title: Second distinct salary
problems.prompt: Return the second highest distinct salary as salary.
problems.solution: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC OFFSET 1 LIMIT 1
problems.explanation: Distinct matters when salaries tie. This query returns no row if a second distinct salary does not exist.

problems.title: Top earners per department
problems.prompt: Return names of all highest-paid employees in each populated department, ordered by name.
problems.solution: SELECT name FROM (SELECT name,DENSE_RANK() OVER(PARTITION BY department_id ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM employees) t WHERE r=1 ORDER BY name
problems.explanation: DENSE_RANK retains ties. A deterministic single winner would need a different requirement.

problems.title: Above department average
problems.prompt: Return employee names earning above their department average, ordered by name.
problems.solution: SELECT name FROM (SELECT name,salary,AVG(salary) OVER(PARTITION BY department_id) av FROM employees) t WHERE salary>av ORDER BY name
problems.explanation: A window aggregate preserves each employee row while computing the comparison baseline.

problems.title: Employees and managers
problems.prompt: Return every employee name and manager name (NULL for no manager), ordered by employee ID.
problems.solution: SELECT e.name,m.name manager FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m ON m.id=e.manager_id ORDER BY e.id
problems.explanation: A self join gives the two roles separate aliases. LEFT JOIN preserves top-level employees.

problems.title: Departments without employees
problems.prompt: Return department names with no employees, ordered by name.
problems.solution: SELECT d.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id=d.id GROUP BY d.id,d.name HAVING COUNT(e.id)=0 ORDER BY d.name
problems.explanation: COUNT(e.id) is zero for an unmatched department. COUNT(*) would count its outer-join row.

problems.title: Running paid revenue
problems.prompt: For paid orders, return order ID and cumulative revenue ordered by date then ID. Use the same ordering in the window.
problems.solution: SELECT id,SUM(amount) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on,id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)::int running FROM orders WHERE status='paid' ORDER BY ordered_on,id
problems.explanation: An explicit ROWS frame and unique ordering make ties on the same day deterministic.

problems.title: Latest paid order per customer
problems.prompt: Return customer ID and their latest paid order ID. Break same-day ties with larger order ID. Order by customer ID.
problems.solution: SELECT customer_id,id FROM (SELECT customer_id,id,ROW_NUMBER() OVER(PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY ordered_on DESC,id DESC) r FROM orders WHERE status='paid') t WHERE r=1 ORDER BY customer_id
problems.explanation: ROW_NUMBER chooses exactly one row per group; the ID tie-breaker is essential.

problems.title: Daily paid revenue
problems.prompt: Return paid revenue by date, ordered by date. Format date as YYYY-MM-DD text.
problems.solution: SELECT to_char(ordered_on,'YYYY-MM-DD') AS revenue_day,SUM(amount)::int revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY ordered_on ORDER BY ordered_on
problems.explanation: Group by date after filtering paid orders. Cast totals here to keep the fixture output type simple.

problems.title: Day-over-day revenue change
problems.prompt: Return each paid-revenue date and change from the previous available date. First change is NULL.
problems.solution: WITH daily AS(SELECT ordered_on,SUM(amount)::int revenue FROM orders WHERE status='paid' GROUP BY ordered_on) SELECT to_char(ordered_on,'YYYY-MM-DD') AS revenue_day,revenue-LAG(revenue) OVER(ORDER BY ordered_on) change FROM daily ORDER BY ordered_on
problems.explanation: Aggregate first, then LAG the daily totals. Missing calendar dates would need a date spine if required.

problems.title: Duplicate salaries
problems.prompt: Return each repeated salary and its employee count, ordered by salary.
problems.solution: SELECT salary,COUNT(*)::int n FROM employees GROUP BY salary HAVING COUNT(*)>1 ORDER BY salary
problems.explanation: Grouping identifies repeated values. This detects salary ties, not duplicate employee records.

problems.title: Paid and cancelled counts
problems.prompt: Return counts of paid and cancelled orders in one row.
problems.solution: SELECT COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE status='paid')::int paid,COUNT(*) FILTER(WHERE status='cancelled')::int cancelled FROM orders
problems.explanation: PostgreSQL FILTER applies a separate condition to each aggregate without dropping the other rows.

problems.title: Department salary totals
problems.prompt: Return each department name and salary total, including empty departments as 0. Order by department ID.
problems.solution: SELECT d.name,COALESCE(SUM(e.salary),0)::int total FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.department_id=d.id GROUP BY d.id,d.name ORDER BY d.id
problems.explanation: Preserve departments with LEFT JOIN and replace a NULL sum with zero.

problems.title: Customers with cancelled and paid orders
problems.prompt: Return names of customers with at least one paid and one cancelled order, ordered by name.
problems.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid') AND EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='cancelled') ORDER BY c.name
problems.explanation: Two EXISTS predicates express both requirements without multiplying rows in a pair of joins.

problems.title: Top two distinct salaries in Engineering
problems.prompt: Return employee names with either of Engineering's top two distinct salaries, ordered by salary descending then ID.
problems.solution: SELECT name FROM (SELECT id,name,salary,DENSE_RANK() OVER(ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM employees WHERE department_id=1) t WHERE r<=2 ORDER BY salary DESC,id
problems.explanation: Top two salary values can include more than two people. ROW_NUMBER would instead cap employee count.

problems.title: Customers with no paid orders
problems.prompt: Return names of customers with no paid orders, including customers with no orders at all. Order by name.
problems.solution: SELECT c.name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id=c.id AND o.status='paid') ORDER BY c.name
problems.explanation: Only paid orders disqualify a customer; move the status filter inside the correlated subquery.
